Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Space Mission Design Game. Engineering figures are real-world values simplified for play: solar flux follows the inverse-square law, one-way light time to Mars reaches ~22 minutes, Mars launch windows recur every ~26 months, and NASA design practice carries roughly 30% mass and power margins. Full source list lives in the challenge's official Resources tab.

HOW TO FLY

WASD / ←↑↓→ moveMouse aimHold click / J sensor pulse Space dash (invulnerable)P pause Stand in green rings to work the station tasks. Bank science at the comms console during a DSN pass. PULSE is your instrument beam — a LIDAR / spectrometer pulse: measure a debris hazard until it resolves; point-blank, the same input works your capture arm — contact measurement and sample capture. Final burn: hold BURN / B in the ring, release in the green — the beam locks out while you burn.

    ONE ENGINEER · TWELVE DISCIPLINES — RANKS EARNED BY FLYING, NEVER BY FIGHTING

    One Engineer, Twelve Disciplines — Your Skill Tree

    You are the relief Flight Dynamics Engineer — the one astronaut on this shift, and the only character in this story. The twelve disciplines below are your own skills, growing run after run, in this exact order: the six flight disciplines, then mechanical engineering, materials science, electrical engineering, biology and medicine — and finally robotics, the endgame, where the robots you build and program take over your tasks. Real astronauts are engineers of many fields in a single person, and every rank makes you personally more capable — able to do more tasks, with more margin. Alone out here, you grow the castaway's way: one solved survival problem at a time — science is the way out. Ranks rise only on successful missions in each discipline's own domain — and every rank is an engineering number you can see in the forge before you commit.

    Reset clears your discipline ranks, mastered contracts and best scores on this device. Nothing is deleted until you confirm.
    ORBITAL LABORATORY — TWO-BURN TRANSFER PLANNER

    Plan the orbit before you price the ship

    Pick a body and a target altitude. The lab flies a Hohmann transfer from a 100 km parking orbit with JPL physical constants (Moon GM 4902.800 km³/s², radius 1737.4 km · Mars 42828.37362 / 3389.5 km · Europa 3202.71210 / 1560.80 km), prices both burns, and turns the total Δv into propellant with the rocket equation — then checks the wet mass against your selected launcher. Honest limits: this is a simplified two-body model. It is not GMAT integration — no perturbations, no third body, no porkchop search.

    Constants: JPL SSD satellite physical parameters ↗ · planetary parameters ↗ · method: NASA Basics of Space Flight, Ch. 4 ↗
